paragraphs: The paper studies how to accelerate SVRG and Katyusha X, two optimization methods used to fit models by minimizing average training loss. Both already reduce the noise associated with stochastic optimization while keeping memory requirements modest. The proposed improvement changes the geometry of their optimization steps through fixed preconditioners.

Preconditioning makes the subproblem within each training epoch harder to solve. The central result is that these subproblems need not be solved exactly: a fixed number of simple computational routines is sufficient to preserve overall convergence. This makes the extra work compatible with provable improvements in both iteration complexity and gradient complexity.

The analysis permits individual terms in the training objective to be nonconvex, provided their sum is strongly convex. That distinction defines the scope of the result: the guarantee depends on the combined objective. In numerical experiments, the authors report average speedups of eightfold in iteration count and sevenfold in runtime, supporting the practical value of the inexact approach.
icml-2019-acceleration-of-svrg-and-katyu.tldr: Inexact preconditioning provably accelerates SVRG and Katyusha X while allowing their harder internal subproblems to be solved approximately.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a physical attack that changes what a camera sees by placing a specially designed sticker over its lens. The target object itself need not be altered. The question is whether one camera modification can cause objects of a chosen type to be classified as a different, attacker-selected class.

The sticker is mostly translucent and produces inconspicuous changes across the observed images. Designing it requires accounting for both the classifier and physical feasibility. The authors use an iterative procedure that updates the adversarial perturbation alongside the threat model, adjusting the description of allowable changes so the resulting attack can actually be realized.

The authors demonstrate physically realizable targeted attacks against ImageNet classifiers, reporting success in 49.6% of cases. The shared camera modification makes the perturbation universal across observations, but the reported success rate does not imply that every image is fooled. The contribution expands the physical attack surface considered in robust machine learning to include manipulation of the imaging device.
icml-2019-adversarial-camera-stickers-a-.tldr: A mostly translucent camera-lens sticker can produce reusable physical perturbations that make classifiers assign attacker-chosen labels.

paragraphs: Alternating minimization tackles an optimization problem by updating different groups of variables in turn. Its simple implementation and strong practical performance have made it useful for large nonconvex problems. This paper asks what kind of stationary solution the method reaches, going beyond the first-order convergence results already available.

The authors analyze both standard alternating minimization and its proximal variant. Under assumptions on the nonconvex objective described as mild, they show that random initialization leads both algorithms to avoid strict saddle points almost surely. Such points are stationary but have a direction of negative curvature, so first-order stationarity alone does not exclude them.

Combining this saddle-avoidance result with known first-order convergence results yields convergence to a second-order stationary point. This gives a stronger characterization of the algorithms’ destinations and resolves an open question about their behavior. The conclusion remains conditional on the stated assumptions and random initialization; second-order stationarity is also a different claim from finding a globally best solution.
icml-2019-alternating-minimizations-conv.tldr: Under mild objective assumptions and random initialization, standard and proximal alternating minimization avoid strict saddles and converge to second-order stationary points.

paragraphs: Attention lets a model select information from a collection, such as words in a sentence or locations in an image. Conventional mechanisms operate on individual items at a fixed granularity. Area attention instead allows the model to select groups of adjacent items, making the unit of attention more flexible.

An area follows the structure of the underlying information: its items can be neighboring positions in an image or consecutive positions in a sequence. Learning determines the area’s size and shape dynamically. The mechanism can also work with existing architectures, including multi-head attention, so a model can attend to several areas at once.

The authors evaluate the approach on machine translation at both character and token levels, and on image captioning. They report improvements over strong, state-of-the-art baselines in every evaluated case. These gains are available with a basic parameter-free form of area attention, indicating that changing how information is grouped can help without requiring extra learned parameters in that form of the mechanism.
icml-2019-area-attention-2cb27ea5c3.tldr: Area attention learns to focus on adjacent groups of varying sizes, improving translation and image captioning even in a parameter-free form.

paragraphs: The paper develops Bayesian methods for jointly estimating multiple Gaussian graphical models, which represent relationships among variables. A central challenge is selecting sparse relationship structures while estimating their strengths. Regularization helps remove weak relationships, but it can also introduce bias by shrinking the relationships that remain too strongly.

The authors give Bayesian treatments of the group graphical lasso and fused graphical lasso, then extend them with continuous spike-and-slab priors. This framework supports adaptive shrinkage and model selection together. Its purpose is to let the amount of shrinkage adjust during inference while determining which relationships belong in the resulting models.

An expectation-maximization algorithm explores posterior modes quickly and dynamically, providing a computational procedure for finding candidate models. The authors report efficient, automatic sparse-model selection with substantially less bias than alternative regularization procedures. Simulations and two real-data examples demonstrate the methods’ performance. The contribution therefore combines a more adaptive statistical formulation with an algorithm designed to make that formulation practical.
icml-2019-bayesian-joint-spike-and-slab-.tldr: Bayesian spike-and-slab extensions of joint graphical lasso combine adaptive shrinkage and sparse-model selection with reduced estimation bias.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decisions that must satisfy an overall budget, such as a total consumption constraint or a reliability requirement. An existing impossibility result creates a difficulty: when an adversary chooses the budget functions, an agent cannot generally achieve no regret under the original comparison standard.

The authors change that standard by introducing a K-benchmark. This comparator must respect the budget within every window of K rounds, rather than only across the entire horizon. The choice of K therefore controls how demanding the comparator’s budget obligations are and changes what performance the learning agent is asked to match.

When K equals the full horizon T, the earlier impossibility result returns. When K grows more slowly than T, expressed as K=o(T), the authors show that regret can be minimized while satisfying long-term budget constraints. Their Cautious Online Lagrangiant Descent policy comes with explicit bounds on regret and remaining budget violations, making the relationship between comparison strength and budget control mathematically concrete.
icml-2019-cautious-regret-minimization-o.tldr: Requiring budget feasibility over shorter comparator windows enables regret minimization with long-term budget control despite adversarial budget functions.

paragraphs: Stochastic bandit algorithms learn which actions to choose from the rewards they observe. This makes reward data a potential route for manipulating future decisions. The paper studies that vulnerability through both offline poisoning of recorded rewards and online attacks that adapt as the learning process unfolds.

For the offline setting, the authors introduce an attack framework and study attacks formulated through convex optimization against several popular bandit algorithms. They show that small changes to rewards in the data can make an algorithm choose an attacker-selected arm with high probability. The result connects corruption of learning evidence to control over the learner’s behavior.

For the online setting, the authors propose an adaptive strategy that does not require knowledge of the bandit algorithm. In their attack framework, it can induce regret that grows linearly while the attacker’s cost grows only logarithmically. This mismatch means sustained damage to learning can require comparatively slow growth in attack expenditure, demonstrating a significant security concern for systems that trust observed rewards.
icml-2019-data-poisoning-attacks-on-stoc.tldr: Reward poisoning can steer stochastic bandits toward attacker-chosen actions and induce linear regret at logarithmic attack cost.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing often produces several noisy labels for the same item, leaving an aggregation model to infer the underlying annotation. Such models commonly account for differences in worker reliability. This paper argues that they also need to capture correlations between workers, which existing approaches do not adequately represent in practical settings.

The proposed enhanced Bayesian classifier combination model, or EBCC, introduces a mixture of reliability patterns within each class. This construction induces dependence between workers and connects the model to item clustering and tensor decomposition. Inference uses a mean-field variational approach, providing a computational way to estimate the model from the collected labels.

The authors report that EBCC avoids two problems affecting existing correlation models: intractable treatment of missing labels and poor scaling to large groups of workers. Across 17 real-world datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy in a comparison involving 10 benchmark crowdsourcing methods. That aggregate finding supports the value of modeling worker relationships without claiming that EBCC wins on every individual dataset.
icml-2019-exploiting-worker-correlation-.tldr: EBCC models correlations among crowd workers while handling missing labels and large worker groups, achieving the highest mean accuracy in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior with a distribution that is easier to work with. Natural-gradient methods can make this optimization fast and simple, but computational obstacles have largely confined their use to minimal exponential-family approximations. Those restrictions limit the kinds of posterior shapes the approximation can represent.

The paper extends natural-gradient inference to structured approximations, including mixtures of exponential-family distributions. Mixtures can represent several modes, making them useful for complex posteriors that a single unimodal approximation may fit poorly. The key step is a minimal conditional exponential-family representation, from which the authors derive simple natural-gradient update rules.

Empirical comparisons show faster convergence than black-box gradient-based methods. The result combines a richer approximation family with an optimization method that remains straightforward to update. Its significance is that using a more expressive posterior approximation need not rule out the computational advantages of natural gradients; the reported experiments support this combination, while the representation supplies the methodological basis for it.
icml-2019-fast-and-simple-natural-gradie.tldr: A conditional exponential-family representation enables simple natural-gradient updates for mixture approximations and faster convergence in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A model can lose accuracy when deployed on data whose statistics differ from its training data. Domain generalization aims to prepare a model for unseen domains without needing target-domain examples to drive adaptation. Many approaches encourage broadly useful features by adding manually designed auxiliary losses during training.

This paper instead learns the auxiliary loss itself through a learning-to-learn approach. The aim is to discover a training signal that helps the feature representation generalize. This moves part of the design problem from selecting a fixed loss by hand to learning how feature training should be guided.

The authors also study heterogeneous domain generalization, where unseen domains contain categories outside the label spaces of the training domains. Here the desired output is a feature representation useful for both new data and new categories. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in conventional and heterogeneous settings. These results support the learned-loss approach for representation transfer under both kinds of change, rather than only shifts among familiar categories.
icml-2019-feature-critic-networks-for-he.tldr: Feature-Critic learns an auxiliary training loss that improves feature generalization to unseen domains, including domains with new categories.

paragraphs: The paper studies when an Ising model permits efficient statistical inference and sampling. Its definition of tractability requires computing the partition function in polynomial time. The partition function summarizes the weights of all configurations, and tractability in the setting considered also permits generating model configurations in polynomial time.

The authors begin with algorithms for planar zero-field Ising models, the basic tractable case. They then extend the approach using the structure of a graph’s triconnected components. Their algorithms apply when each of these components is either planar or has a size bounded by a constant, allowing a larger graph to contain certain nonplanar pieces.

A particular consequence is polynomial-time inference and sampling for zero-field Ising models whose graphs exclude K3,3 as a minor. This family extends beyond planar graphs and can have unbounded genus, a measure of topological complexity. The finding therefore broadens tractability beyond planarity while retaining a specific structural restriction on the graph and the zero-field condition on the model.
icml-2019-inference-and-sampling-of-k-33.tldr: Structural graph decomposition extends polynomial-time inference and sampling to zero-field Ising models with K3,3-minor-free graphs.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes account for uncertainty in the model used to make sequential decisions. That uncertainty can come from model mismatch, approximation errors, or adversarial behavior. The paper focuses on making this framework useful in large or continuous state spaces, where representing everything exactly is difficult.

Function approximation helps address scale, but it can introduce additional mismatch and uncertainty. Earlier results for state aggregation showed that robust policies can have tighter performance bounds because they are less sensitive to approximation errors. The authors extend this line of analysis to the substantially broader class of kernel-based approximators.

The paper provides analytical and empirical evidence that robust policies can significantly outperform corresponding non-robust policies. The claim is about a possible benefit supported by the analysis and experiments, rather than an unconditional advantage in every problem. Its practical meaning is that robustness can address uncertainty introduced by the approximation machinery itself, making it relevant to the process of scaling reinforcement learning as well as to external disturbances.
icml-2019-kernel-based-reinforcement-lea.tldr: The paper extends robustness results to kernel-based reinforcement learning and shows that robust policies can substantially outperform non-robust counterparts.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a system on tasks that arrive sequentially or as a stream. A major difficulty is catastrophic forgetting: learning later tasks can damage performance on earlier ones. This paper proposes a framework that addresses the problem by explicitly considering how a neural network’s structure should evolve.

The framework separates two components. One optimizes the neural structure, while the other learns or fine-tunes the parameters. This separation makes the choice of structure an explicit part of continual learning, rather than treating the network only as a fixed collection of values to update. The authors describe the resulting structural evolution as intuitively meaningful.

Experiments show strong ability to alleviate forgetting, and the method outperforms all compared baselines on permuted MNIST, split CIFAR100, and Visual Domain Decathlon in the continual-learning setting. These findings support structure learning as a useful companion to parameter learning. The reported result is a reduction in forgetting and better comparative performance, rather than a claim that forgetting is eliminated in every task sequence.
icml-2019-learn-to-grow-a-continual-stru.tldr: Separating neural structure optimization from parameter learning helps reduce catastrophic forgetting and improves performance on three continual-learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: NATTACK tests neural-network robustness without accessing internal layers or weights. Its central choice is to learn a distribution of adversarial inputs around a benign example. Instead of seeking one optimal perturbation directly, it seeks a probability density from which a sampled input is likely to cause a classification error.

The distribution is confined to a small region centered on the original input. A single attack algorithm can be applied to different neural networks, including ordinary models and models produced by defense techniques. This gives the method a common framework for evaluating defenses whose internal computations need not be available to the attacker.

Tests cover two ordinary networks and 13 defended networks. NATTACK outperforms state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks in most reported test cases. The experiments also identify adversarial training as one of the strongest defenses tested and find that adversarial examples transfer less readily between defended networks than between ordinary ones. These are comparative empirical findings, not guarantees that the attack defeats every defense.
icml-2019-nattack-learning-the-distribut.tldr: NATTACK learns local distributions of adversarial examples without model internals and outperforms competing attacks in most reported tests.

paragraphs: Robustness certification seeks a region around an input within which adversarial changes cannot alter the model’s decision. This paper studies regions whose permitted changes differ across input features. Such non-uniform bounds can describe the local decision boundary more flexibly than bounds that impose the same allowance on every feature.

The authors formulate the search for these regions as an optimization problem with nonlinear constraints. They propose a framework for general feedforward networks that bounds the output logits, the scores used to make predictions. These bounds allow a relaxed version of the optimization problem to be solved using an augmented Lagrangian method.

In experiments, the non-uniform certified regions have greater volume than uniform ones. Robust models produce still larger non-uniform bounds than normal models and offer better interpretability in the reported comparisons. The authors also use geometric similarity among the bounds to define a quantitative, data-agnostic measure of feature robustness. The contribution thus connects certification with a more detailed description of how robustness varies across features.
icml-2019-on-certifying-non-uniform-boun.tldr: Feature-specific robustness bounds certify larger regions in experiments and reveal more detailed geometry of neural-network decision boundaries.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes algorithms for regularized optimal transport between two discrete probability distributions, each supported on at most n points. It considers Greenkhorn, a greedy variant of Sinkhorn, and develops a family of adaptive accelerated methods. The goal is to establish stronger computational guarantees while explaining favorable practical behavior.

For Greenkhorn, the authors improve the known complexity bound from roughly n²/ε³ to n²/ε², with logarithmic factors suppressed. This matches the best known Sinkhorn bound. The improvement concerns the theoretical dependence on accuracy ε and helps account for Greenkhorn’s practical performance, without establishing a universally better worst-case bound than Sinkhorn.

A primal-dual analysis and a tight bound on the dual solution also lead to adaptive primal-dual accelerated mirror descent algorithms. Their complexity is roughly n²√γ/ε, where γ lies in (0,n] and depends on constants in the Bregman divergence. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show favorable performance for both Greenkhorn and the accelerated family, complementing the theoretical analysis.
icml-2019-on-efficient-optimal-transport.tldr: Sharper analysis improves Greenkhorn’s complexity guarantee and yields adaptive accelerated mirror descent algorithms for regularized optimal transport.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an online ranking model that learns from clicks while using features describing the available items. It separates the probability of a click into two parts: whether an item is examined and how attractive it is. This distinction allows the model to account for exposure as well as item appeal.

Attractiveness is assumed to be a linear function of an item’s feature vector and an unknown parameter. The examination function is subject to assumptions described as relatively mild. The authors develop and analyze an algorithm for this setting, using the feature-based structure to change how the learning problem scales.

The analysis replaces dependence on the number of items with dependence on the feature dimension. This matters when a large collection can be described through a comparatively compact set of features. In the special orthogonal case, the algorithm also improves on the state-of-the-art regret guarantee. That stronger comparison is specific to the stated reduction, while the broader contribution is a feature-based framework for handling many items.
icml-2019-online-learning-to-rank-with-f.tldr: A feature-based online ranking algorithm replaces item-count dependence with feature-dimension dependence and improves regret in the orthogonal case.

paragraphs: The paper considers gradients of expectations over discrete outcomes. Computing such a gradient directly can require summing over every category, which becomes intractable when the category set is very large or countably infinite. Stochastic gradient estimators offer a way to work with these problems without performing the full summation.

The authors introduce a technique that reduces the variance of any such estimator while leaving its bias unchanged. In particular, an estimator that is unbiased remains unbiased after the transformation. The method is an instance of Rao-Blackwellization, connecting the proposed improvement to a statistical principle for making estimators less noisy.

The distinction between bias and variance is central to the contribution: reducing random fluctuation does not require changing the estimator’s systematic error. This makes the technique applicable as an improvement to existing estimators, rather than only as a replacement designed for one task. The authors demonstrate its benefits on semi-supervised classification and pixel attention, providing practical evidence alongside the general estimator-level result.
icml-2019-rao-blackwellized-stochastic-g.tldr: Rao-Blackwellization reduces the variance of stochastic gradients for discrete expectations while preserving their original bias, including unbiasedness.

paragraphs: Learning a linear model from little data can benefit from knowing the direction in which each feature should influence the prediction. The paper introduces STEW, a regularization method designed to use this kind of prior knowledge. It shrinks feature weights toward one another, with an equal-weights solution emerging as regularization becomes infinitely strong.

The authors provide theoretical results about the equal-weights solution to explain how this strategy can balance bias and variance. The approach restricts differences between weights, allowing the model to trade some flexibility for more stable estimation. This gives the equal-weights endpoint a role in understanding the behavior of the full regularized model.

Across learning problems including Tetris, STEW outperforms ridge regression, Lasso, and non-negative Lasso when feature directions are known. It also remains competitive enough to outperform alternatives under diverse conditions with unreliable or absent directions. The Tetris results use a new approach based on multinomial logistic regression for sequential decisions, extending the evaluation beyond ordinary prediction tasks.
icml-2019-regularization-in-directable-e.tldr: STEW regularizes linear models by pulling weights together, using feature-direction knowledge to improve learning from small datasets.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning seeks learning procedures that work across a distribution of decision-making tasks. Estimating the policy gradients needed for this training can be difficult: large Hessian calculations, noisy estimates, poor sample efficiency, and unstable training all create obstacles. This paper focuses on improving those gradient estimates without introducing bias.

Taming MAML, or TMAML, defines a surrogate objective that incorporates control variates into gradient estimation through automatic differentiation. These control variates reduce variance while preserving unbiasedness. The authors also propose a version that learns the control variates through the meta-learning framework itself, supporting efficient and scalable training across a distribution of Markov decision processes.

The empirical study compares TMAML with MAML and several approaches addressing the variance-bias trade-off, including DICE, LVC, and action-dependent control variates. The authors report better gradient variance and estimation accuracy, together with higher performance across challenging meta reinforcement learning environments. The findings connect the quality of the training signal to practical learning performance, while retaining an unbiased estimation objective.
icml-2019-taming-maml-efficient-unbiased.tldr: TMAML uses control variates in an automatically differentiated surrogate objective to reduce meta reinforcement learning gradient variance without adding bias.

paragraphs: This paper asks which fairness properties can emerge from ordinary machine learning without explicit fairness constraints. Its central result concerns group calibration: once a prediction score is known, group membership provides no further information about the outcome. The authors show that unconstrained learning implies this property in many settings.

The analysis supplies an upper bound and a matching lower bound that establishes its optimality. This gives a quantitative foundation for viewing calibration as a possible consequence of learning itself. It challenges the assumption that achieving group calibration always requires a separate intervention, while retaining the qualification that the result applies in the settings studied.

The same analysis reveals tension with two other fairness criteria, separation and independence. As the learned score’s excess risk decreases, the authors prove that violations of those criteria become stronger. Better predictive optimization therefore does not imply simultaneous progress on all fairness definitions. The paper clarifies which fairness behavior unconstrained learning can produce and why calibration alone cannot stand in for every fairness objective.
icml-2019-the-implicit-fairness-criterio.tldr: In many settings, unconstrained learning produces group calibration while lower excess risk strengthens violations of separation and independence.

paragraphs: Random Fourier features help scale kernel methods, but earlier theory often focused on individual tasks and predicted more demanding requirements than experiments suggested. This paper develops a unified risk analysis covering squared-error and Lipschitz-continuous losses. It makes the trade-off between computation and expected risk depend on the problem’s regularization and effective degrees of freedom.

For standard random Fourier features, the authors improve bounds on how many features are needed to retain the corresponding minimax risk convergence rate of kernel ridge regression. They also analyze a data-dependent alternative that samples features according to ridge leverage scores. This choice further reduces the required number of features.

Computing the leverage scores is itself expensive, so the paper introduces a simple approximation scheme. The authors prove that it reduces computational cost without sacrificing statistical efficiency. The overall contribution connects feature counts, sampling choices, and approximation cost within one analysis, helping explain how computational savings can coexist with strong statistical convergence guarantees.
icml-2019-towards-a-unified-analysis-of-.tldr: A unified risk analysis sharpens random-feature requirements and supports cheaper leverage-based sampling without loss of statistical efficiency.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. A common strategy aligns their feature distributions. This paper highlights a potential problem: suppressing domain-specific variation can distort those distributions and worsen adaptability, measured through the expected risk of an ideal hypothesis shared by both domains.

Transferable Adversarial Training addresses this by generating examples that bridge the source and target domains. It then adversarially trains the classifier to make consistent predictions over those examples. The approach is designed to support transfer without relying on feature-distribution distortion to produce domain-invariant representations, and it algorithmically guarantees the adaptability component of the theoretical learning bound.

Experiments cover vision and language tasks, including object recognition, transfer from synthetic to real data, and sentiment classification. The authors report advances over state-of-the-art methods across these adaptation tasks. The contribution joins a concern about the theoretical conditions for successful transfer with a training procedure that directly addresses it, supported by empirical comparisons across different application types.
icml-2019-transferable-adversarial-train.tldr: Transferable Adversarial Training bridges domains with generated examples and prediction consistency while preserving adaptability in the theoretical bound.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference uses a finite collection of particles to construct flexible Bayesian approximations. This paper studies these methods through Wasserstein gradient flows, a perspective that describes how probability distributions move during optimization. The aim is both to explain existing methods and to derive practical improvements from that explanation.

The authors unify several finite-particle approximations and show that their approximation amounts to a necessary smoothing operation, expressible in two equivalent forms. This interpretation exposes relationships and assumptions among existing methods and motivates new ones. It gives apparently different particle procedures a common theoretical description based on how finite representations introduce smoothing.

Building on this theory, the paper proposes an acceleration framework and a principled method for selecting bandwidths for general particle-based variational inference. Both use the geometry of Wasserstein space. Experiments report improved convergence from acceleration and better sample accuracy from bandwidth selection. These results connect the theoretical interpretation to two separate practical concerns: how quickly the particles progress and how accurately their final arrangement represents the target.
icml-2019-understanding-and-accelerating.tldr: A Wasserstein-flow analysis unifies particle-based variational methods and yields acceleration and bandwidth selection that improve experimental performance.

paragraphs: Langevin dynamics already has a useful interpretation as a gradient flow of KL divergence in Wasserstein space. That perspective supports convergence analysis and has inspired particle-based variational inference. This paper develops a broader geometric framework intended to explain general MCMC dynamics through flows of probability distributions.

The framework represents these dynamics as a fiber-gradient Hamiltonian flow on Wasserstein space over a fiber-Riemannian Poisson manifold. Its central explanatory feature is a decomposition combining conservation and convergence. This structure separates complementary aspects of the dynamics and provides a clearer account of their behavior within a common mathematical description.

The framework also allows MCMC dynamics to be simulated through particle-based variational inference. This creates a route for enriching particle methods with more efficient dynamics while bringing their advantages to MCMC. The authors construct two particle-based methods for a particular MCMC dynamics and demonstrate benefits experimentally. The practical examples support the framework’s ability to generate algorithms, alongside its broader theoretical contribution to understanding sampling dynamics.
icml-2019-understanding-mcmc-dynamics-as.tldr: A geometric framework describes general MCMC dynamics through conservation and convergence and enables new particle-based variational simulations.
